content: Diarrhoea is a significant cause of mortality, particularly among children in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), accounting for approximately 1.8 million deaths annually. One of the strategies identified to mitigate this burden is the promotion of hand-washing practices. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of hand-washing promotion interventions on the incidence of diarrhoeal episodes in both children and adults. To conduct this analysis, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, as well as the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trial Registry Platform (ICTRP) and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT). The search was completed on January 8, 2020. Additional studies were identified through reference checking, citation searching, and direct contact with study authors. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs that compared hand-washing interventions with no intervention in terms of their effects on diarrhoea episodes. Three independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The analysis was stratified by setting: child day-care centres or schools, community-based settings, and hospital-based settings. Where appropriate, incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were pooled using the generic inverse variance method and a random-effects model, with a 95% confidence interval (CI). The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 29 RCTs were included in the analysis. These comprised 13 trials conducted in child day-care centres or schools, primarily in high-income countries (54,471 participants), 15 community-based trials in LMICs (29,347 participants), and one hospital-based trial involving individuals with AIDS in a high-income country (148 participants). All trials were of short-term duration. In child day-care centres or schools in high-income countries, hand-washing promotion, which included educational activities and sometimes the provision of soap, reduced diarrhoea episodes by approximately one-third (IRR 0.70, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.85; 9 trials, 4664 participants; high-certainty evidence). In LMICs, a similar reduction was observed, but this was based on only two trials conducted in urban Egypt and Kenya (IRR 0.66, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.99; 2 trials, 45,380 participants; low-certainty evidence). Behavioural changes were reported in only four trials, and the methods of data collection were prone to bias. For example, in one trial from the USA, hand-washing behaviour improved, while in a trial from Kenya where free soap was provided, hand-washing frequency did not increase, but soap use did (data not pooled; 3 trials, 1845 participants; low-certainty evidence). In community-based settings in LMICs, hand-washing promotion likely reduced diarrhoea episodes by about one-quarter (IRR 0.71, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.81; 9 trials, 15,950 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, six of these nine trials were conducted in Asia, with only one trial from South America and two from sub-Saharan Africa. In seven trials where soap was provided alongside hand-washing education, the effect size was greater (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.75; 7 trials, 12,646 participants) compared to trials with education alone (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.05; 2 trials, 3304 participants). Intervention groups demonstrated increased hand-washing at critical times (e.g., before eating, after using the toilet, or after cleaning a baby’s bottom) and greater adherence to hand-hygiene procedures compared to control groups (data not pooled; 4 trials, 3591 participants; high-certainty evidence). In the single hospital-based trial conducted among a high-risk population (individuals with AIDS), hand-washing promotion significantly reduced the mean number of diarrhoeal episodes by 1.68 episodes in the intervention group compared to the control group (mean difference −1.68, 95% CI −1.93 to −1.43; 1 trial, 148 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Hand-washing frequency in the intervention group increased to seven times per day, compared to three times per day in the control group (1 trial, 148 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). No trials were identified that evaluated the effects of hand-washing promotion on diarrhoea-related mortality or cost-effectiveness. In conclusion, hand-washing promotion likely reduces diarrhoea episodes by approximately 30% in child day-care centres in high-income countries and among communities in LMICs. However, the included trials do not provide evidence regarding the long-term impact of these interventions.
